items.title: Kubeflow Pipelines: Reflected XSS in the frontend pod information and events error responses
items.description:
## Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines frontend reflected untrusted pod names and namespaces into HTML error responses from the pod-information and pod-events routes. An attacker could craft a link that causes JavaScript to execute in the frontend's origin when a user follows it and reaches an affected error response.

Affected routes include `/pipeline/k8s/pod` and `/pipeline/k8s/pod/events` (the deployment's configured base path may differ).

## Impact and prerequisites

Successful exploitation requires a victim to open an attacker-supplied link and reach the vulnerable response. JavaScript execution may expose information accessible to the victim's browser or perform actions in the application's origin.

items.description:
## Summary

Kubeflow Pipelines API server does not sufficiently validate SQL identifier fields decoded from the `page_token` pagination parameter. Client-controlled fields can reach SQL query construction, allowing SQL injection through list APIs.

This advisory consolidates the original pipeline-listing report and the later run-listing report in [GHSA-mhpc-2x8q-2vp9](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/security/advisories/GHSA-mhpc-2x8q-2vp9). Their contributions and chronology are distinguished below.

## Impact and prerequisites

An attacker able to invoke an affected list API may read data accessible to the API server's database account, including data belonging to other namespaces. The original report demonstrated database read access through an authenticated Kubeflow deployment.

items.title: Kubeflow Pipelines: RBAC bypass on shared pipelines allows any authenticated user to delete or modify global pipelines
items.description:
## Summary

In multi-user mode, the Kubeflow Pipelines API server skipped authorization checks for shared/global pipelines with an empty namespace. This exception applied to write and delete operations as well as reads, allowing an authenticated user to modify or delete shared pipelines without the required Kubernetes RBAC permissions.

## Impact

Unauthorized modification compromises the integrity of shared pipeline definitions and versions. Unauthorized deletion can make shared pipelines unavailable.

Execution of a modified pipeline can cause attacker-controlled workload behavior, but this is a conditional downstream consequence requiring the modified pipeline to be executed. Modification alone does not demonstrate immediate worker code execution.

items.title: Kubeflow Pipelines — API server fetches a caller-supplied pipelineURL without host validation
items.description:
## Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines API server fetched caller-supplied pipeline package URLs without restricting the destination. A caller authorized to create a pipeline or pipeline version could cause requests to originate from the API server's network position, including to internal services that the caller could not otherwise reach.

## Impact

The reported evidence demonstrates blind server-side request forgery and a limited status-code oracle. The fetched response is processed as a pipeline package; the report does not demonstrate arbitrary response-body disclosure or credential theft. A request to a cloud metadata endpoint returned HTTP 403, which does not establish access to metadata contents or tokens.

items.title: Kubeflow Pipelines: Cross-tenant execution-cache poisoning / output substitution via a namespace-blind cache key in the cache webhook (multi-user)
items.description:
## Summary

The legacy Kubeflow Pipelines V1/raw-Argo execution cache does not separate cached results by Kubernetes namespace. In multi-user deployments where tenants share the cache service, a tenant can receive another tenant's cached outputs or seed outputs that are subsequently substituted into another tenant's step.

This affects the Argo-template cache mutating webhook and its cache-server storage path. Standard KFP V2 component pods bypass this webhook cache; the separate V2 cache implementation is outside this advisory's scope.

## Affected deployments and impact

The issue requires multiple tenant namespaces sharing the legacy cache service, cache-enabled V1/raw-Argo steps, and cache entries that satisfy the configured staleness policy. The standard multi-user configuration watches pods across namespaces.

items.title: Claude Code: TOCTOU Race in Edit Tool Allows File Writes Outside the Workspace
items.description:
Claude Code validated Edit tool targets using point-in-time pathname and symlink resolution that was not bound to the underlying directory inodes or file descriptors. On macOS, a process running inside Claude Code's Bash sandbox could exploit the resulting time-of-check to time-of-use window by atomically swapping an in-workspace parent directory with a symlink after validation completed, causing the unsandboxed Edit implementation to overwrite an attacker-selected user-writable file outside the workspace. Exploiting this required the ability to run attacker-controlled code inside the sandbox, such as through a malicious repository or dependency script.

Users on standard Claude Code auto-update have received this fix automatically. Users performing manual updates are advised to update to the latest version.

Claude Code thanks hackerone.com/mahoraga007 (Sunder Singh) for reporting this

items.title: croc: Overwrite-confirmation bypass via a crafted "croc-stdin-" filename on receive
items.description:
## Summary

croc is an end-to-end encrypted peer-to-peer file transfer tool. On the receiving side, the confirmation that normally protects an existing file from being overwritten or resumed is skipped whenever the received file's name starts with `croc-stdin-`, regardless of whether the incoming transfer is actually a text transfer. A sender can therefore name a file `croc-stdin-<existing-name>` and silently overwrite, truncate, or replace an existing file of that name in the receiver's working directory - including removing the existing file and substituting a symlink - without the `Overwrite?` prompt that the standard path requires. The exemption was introduced to keep croc's internal text-transfer artifacts from triggering prompts, but it is keyed on the filename prefix rather than on the transfer type, so any ordinary file transfer can claim the exemption.

## Vulnerability Details

items.title: Moleculer: Unauthenticated Denial of Service via negative length field in the TCP transporter packet parser
items.description:
### Summary

The TCP transporter's packet parser (`src/transporters/tcp/parser.js`) reads the packet length field with `Buffer.prototype.readInt32BE`, a signed read. A crafted packet whose length field has the sign bit set yields a negative `length`. The parser then advances past the parsed message with `packet = packet.slice(length)`, but `Buffer.prototype.slice` clamps an out-of-range negative start index to `0`, so the buffer is returned unchanged. The `while (packet.length > 0)` loop condition therefore never becomes false, producing an infinite synchronous loop that blocks the Node.js event loop indefinitely.

### Impact

Any Moleculer node using the TCP transporter can be rendered completely unresponsive by an unauthenticated remote peer sending a single ~10-byte crafted TCP packet, before any protocol handshake or authentication takes place. `TcpReader.onTcpClientConnected` pipes

That metadata is never consulted at runtime: `metadata.go:19` stores it as a string that only the documentation exporter reads (`api/reflect.go:82-110`). items.title: Kubeflow Pipelines API server lacks authorization for shared pipeline uploads
items.description:
## Summary

In multi-user mode, the Kubeflow Pipelines API server's HTTP multipart upload endpoints (`POST /apis/v2beta1/pipelines/upload` and `POST /apis/v2beta1/pipelines/upload_version`) perform no authorization when the target namespace is empty. items.description:

items.description:
### Summary
`GET /batchdownload` streams a batch ZIP to any requester who supplies its `uniqid`, without checking that the current user/session created it. In deployments where users have separate home directories, a valid low-privileged user who obtains an active archive id can download another user's batch archive, disclosing files the per-user boundary otherwise protects. Reported with explicit preconditions and bounded impact — not a universal "any user steals any file" issue.

The archive id is generated with plain `uniqid()` and no ownership metadata is bound to it before streaming.

items.title: Pocket ID: Email verification token remains valid after address change, enabling arbitrary verified-email spoofing
items.description:
## Summary

An authenticated Pocket ID user can request an email-verification token while their account uses an address they control, change the account email address, and then redeem the previously issued token. The token is bound only to the user ID, not to the address to which it was sent, and changing the address does not revoke outstanding tokens.

As a result, Pocket ID marks the newly supplied address as verified even though the user never proved control of it. Pocket ID subsequently returns that address with `email_verified: true` in OIDC claims. A relying party that trusts this claim for email-based account linking or provisioning can therefore link the attacker's Pocket ID identity to a victim's existing account, leading to cross-application account takeover.

This was verified against commit `9f559788a44cfea790de360da0a74d4bdf8ca5d5`.

items.description:
### Summary
The `handle_short_request()` function in `urwid/display/web.py` raises an unhandled `UnicodeEncodeError` when processing a POST request body containing non-ASCII bytes. The function reads POST input and encodes it to ASCII before writing to a named pipe. Any byte value above `0x7F` causes the CGI process to exit with an unhandled exception, returning an HTTP 500 error to the client. Additionally, a file descriptor opened earlier in the same function is not closed before the exception propagates, causing a file descriptor leak for the lifetime of the CGI process.

A second instance of missing exception handling exists in the polling update path, where non-UTF-8 socket output causes an unhandled `UnicodeDecodeError`.

items.description:
### Summary

The documented `web.NewHandler` static file server can read files outside `Config.AppDir` when the request path contains URL-encoded dot-segments such as `%2e%2e`. Go's `ServeMux` redirects plain `/../` paths, but it passes encoded dot-segments to the handler after decoding `r.URL.Path`. ```

items.title: fast-agent: `fast-agent serve` binds HTTP to 0.0.0.0 with no authentication by default; with --shell this is unauthenticated remote command execution
items.description:
## Summary
`fast-agent serve` exposes the agent over MCP. By default it uses HTTP transport bound to `0.0.0.0` (all interfaces) on port 8000 with **no authentication** (`auth=None`) and prints no warning. Any host that can reach the port can call the exposed `agent` tool. When the server is started with `--shell` (which is `-x`, the flag used in the README quickstart `uvx fast-agent mcp@latest -x`), the agent has a local `execute` shell tool, so an unauthenticated remote client can drive the agent into running arbitrary OS commands — unauthenticated RCE.

items.description:
## Summary

Telepresence's Traffic Manager gRPC API (port 8081) requires no authentication. Any pod with cluster-network access to the Traffic Manager can register as a client in an arbitrary managed namespace and create intercepts against services in that namespace, regardless of Kubernetes RBAC. items.description:
## Summary

The Traffic Manager `Tunnel` gRPC streaming endpoint accepts a session ID from the first bytes of the client-controlled message payload. No verification confirms the caller owns the session. An attacker supplying a valid active session ID receives a fully routed tunnel for that session, gaining the network routing capabilities of the legitimate Telepresence client. Tested on HEAD v2.28.0, commit b2231a4.

The `Tunnel` handler reads identity from a client-provided binary payload rather than from a verified credential or prior authenticated gRPC call:

items.title: ezBookkeeping: Source-IP allowlist (MCP & API token) is bypassable via a spoofed `X-Forwarded-For` header
items.description:
### Summary
A remote attacker from any IP address defeats the operator-configured source-IP allowlist (`mcp_allowed_remote_ips` / `api_token_allowed_remote_ips`) by sending a single `X-Forwarded-For: <allowlisted-ip>` header. The router is created with `gin.New()` and never calls `SetTrustedProxies`, so gin trusts every proxy by default and `c.ClientIP()` returns the attacker-supplied header verbatim. The same forged value is also written to `Transaction.CreatedIp` and the access log, so the attacker's real IP never appears in any record.

### Details
`cmd/webserver.go:104` builds the router with `gin.New()`. A grep of `cmd/` and `pkg/` confirms `SetTrustedProxies` is never called, leaving gin's default trusted-proxy range of `0.0.0.0/0` and `::/0`. `WebContext` (`pkg/core/context_web.go:39`) embeds `*gin.Context` and does not override `ClientIP()`.

items.title: Gradle Shadow: Zip Slip path traversal in ShadowCopyAction — no independent entry-name sanitization
items.description:
### Summary
ShadowCopyAction in the Shadow plugin does not validate or sanitize ZIP entry names before writing them to the output fat JAR. A malicious upstream dependency containing path traversal sequences (e.g. `../../../../tmp/pwned.txt`) in entry names will have those entries reproduced verbatim in the output shadow JAR.

### Details
The vulnerability exists because Shadow relies entirely on Gradle's ZipFileTree for entry sanitization rather than implementing its own path validation. This means:

1. Users on Gradle < 7.6.2 / 8.x < 8.2.0 are directly exploitable
2. The produced shadow JAR becomes a Zip Slip weapon against any 
downstream consumer using unprotected extraction (raw ZipInputStream, 
older CI tooling, custom Java unpackers)
3. If Shadow ever uses a non-ZipFileTree code path, protection 
disappears silently

items.title: Remark42: Rate limit bypass via unconditional trust of X-Forwarded-For/X-Real-IP headers in direct-internet deployment
items.description:
### Summary
Remark42 applied chi's `middleware.RealIP` globally, trusting `True-Client-IP` / `X-Real-IP` / `X-Forwarded-For` headers without verifying the request came from a trusted proxy. The per-IP rate limiters key on the overwritten `r.RemoteAddr`, so any client can bypass every per-IP rate limiter by rotating spoofed IP headers. The same spoofed IP also drives other per-IP controls (stored comment IP, anonymous identity derivation, and `--votes-ip` vote de-duplication). This affects deployments reachable directly from the internet (Remark42's built-in HTTP, static TLS, and ACME modes are all documented and supported), as well as any proxied deployment where the proxy forwards an attacker-controlled recognised header.

items.title: Pocket ID: The client credentials grant allows any OIDC client to obtain tokens for arbitrary audiences
items.description:
## Summary

The client credentials grant (`grant_type=client_credentials`) does not validate the resource parameter before embedding it as the aud claim in the issued JWT. Any authenticated OIDC client can obtain a Pocket ID-signed access token claiming authorization for any arbitrary audience, including other registered OIDC clients. There is no check that the requested audience is a registered resource server, and no check that the requesting client has been granted permission to access it.

In `backend/internal/service/oidc_service.go`, `createTokenFromClientCredentials` accepts the resource parameter from the token request and places it directly into the `aud` claim of the issued JWT without validation:

```golang

items.description:
## 1. Executive Summary

JSON-java version 20260522 contains an unguarded path from an HTTP request body to unbounded `BigInteger` and `BigDecimal` construction. `JSONTokener.nextSimpleValue()` accumulates numeric characters into a `StringBuilder` with no length cap, then passes the full string to `JSONObject.stringToNumber()`, which calls `new BigInteger(val)` or `new BigDecimal(val)` directly. Spring Boot has no default size limit for `application/json` request bodies. No parser configuration option (`withStrictMode`, `withKeepStrings`) prevents this. items.title: tsParticles: Unbounded HTTP Request Body Buffering in @tsparticles/mcp-server Leads to Remote DoS
items.description:
### Summary

The HTTP server mode of `@tsparticles/mcp-server` accumulates all incoming request body chunks into an in-memory `Buffer[]` array with no size limit before calling `JSON.parse`. An unauthenticated remote attacker can stream an arbitrarily large body to `POST /mcp`, exhausting the Node.js process memory and causing a Denial of Service. The official Docker image ships with HTTP mode enabled by default (`--port 3000` on `0.0.0.0`), making this exploitable without any special configuration in containerized deployments.

The vulnerability exists in `integrations/mcp-server/src/index.ts` at lines 399–407. The `POST /mcp` request handler resolves a `Promise` that pushes every incoming data chunk into a `Buffer[]` array without checking the cumulative size, a `Content-Length` header, or any other guard:

### Summary
The `readPsd()` function in `ag-psd` accepts a `totalMemoryLimit` option to cap memory usage when parsing untrusted PSD files, but this limit is never forwarded to the layer image buffer allocation path. items.title: zt-zip: ZipUtil.unpack can change file permissions of output directory
items.description:
### Summary
When using one of the `ZipUtil.unpack` overloads, the file permissions of the output directory can be changed. For example, when the output directory was only accessible to the 'owner' it could be instead made accessible to every OS user.

### Details
When the name of a ZIP entry resolves to the output directory itself (e.g. the name `/`), the path traversal checks permit it and then perform actions on that directory, such as applying the file permissions of the ZIP entry to it.

### PoC
This proof of concept requires an OS with support for POSIX file permissions. This issue itself is however not limited to those OS' with POSIX file permissions, see zt-zip's `ZTFilePermissionsUtil.fetchDefaultStrategy` which uses a fallback in that case.

items.title: traQ: Privilege escalation by OAuth prompt=none request
items.description:
In OAuth2 silent authorization (`prompt=none`), when the `scope` parameter was empty or omitted, all scopes registered for the OAuth client became eligible for issuance. However, the prior consent check was performed against the empty requested scope set. As a result, an attacker could obtain an access token with broader scopes than the user had previously consented to, without requiring additional consent.

## Impact

If an attacker controls an OAuth client capable of receiving authorization codes, and a user has already consented to only a subset of that client’s scopes, the attacker may be able to obtain a token containing all scopes registered for that client by sending an authorization request with `prompt=none` and an empty or omitted `scope`.

If the user has not consented to the client at all, `consent_required` is returned as usual.

## Patches

This issue has been fixed in v3.2

items.title: traQ: XSS in the User Uploaded File Retrieval API
items.description:
### Impact

For instances where `TRAQ_STORAGE_TYPE` is set to `local`, the file retrieval API `/files/{fileId}` could serve user-uploaded SVG or HTML files in a way that allowed them to be rendered directly in the browser.

As a result, an attacker who can upload files to traQ could upload a crafted SVG or HTML file and trick a victim into opening the file URL, allowing the attacker to execute arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser.

### Patches

This issue has been fixed in v3.28.3.

After this fix, the file retrieval API always adds the `Content-Disposition` header to its responses regardless of the value of the `dl` query parameter. This prevents user-uploaded files from being displayed directly in the browser.

### Workarounds

To mitigate the impact of this issue, apply either of the following workarounds:

* Change `TRAQ_STORAGE_TYPE` to a storage backend other than `local`.

### Summary
isomorphic-git's tree parser (`src/models/GitTree.js`) validates each entry name only against the path separators `/` and `\`. It does not reject the standalone reserved name `..`, so a malicious repository can, on a single `clone`/`checkout`, **write files outside the working

### Summary

  …
}

items.title: isomorphic-git: Arbitrary file write outside of working tree via directory symlink during checkout (potential RCE)
items.description:
### Summary
`git.checkout` writes working-tree files through a directory **symlink** without checking the leading path, so a malicious repository can write **outside the intended working directory**. The defect is in isomorphic-git's checkout logic itself and is therefore **independent of the `fs` provider**. The *impact* depends on the configured filesystem; worst case is arbitrary file write on the host, e.g. injecting an attacker key into `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` → remote login / code execution.

### Details
A single git tree can't hold a name as both a symlink and a directory, so the attack uses two states:

```
Commit N:    config            (mode 120000, symlink → ../.ssh)
Commit N+1:  config/           (mode 040000, tree)
               authorized_keys (mode 100644, attacker public key)
```
